Spiraling Food Costs

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Spiraling food prices can only deepen the poverty trap, lower nutrition, inhibit education - prospects are dwindling for the poor. What steps can South Africans take to reverse the hunger trend?

Unique Selling Point:
Nutrition is at the heart of a healthy life cycle. Get it right and society can thrive. But get it wrong and the cycle of poverty gets harder to break. The prospects this year are looking bleak for the South African food chain. "Economists are predicting that food prices will rise between 15 and 20% in the coming months. Pushing low income earners to the brink and stretching middle class pockets further". Compared with a year ago consumers are paying nearly 12% more for basic food items, 41.1% more for petrol and 57.5% more for diesel. (According to economist Dawie Roodt). Much of the escalation of prices in our shops is linked to the break down in supplies of commodities like grain and fuel related to the war in Ukraine. So how does one combat these devastating effects on our most basic needs? Must we change our diets? Export less food or raise the taxes on food exports to become more self-sufficient?

Summary:
Society’s ills are reflected by what we eat. We take a look at how malnutrition is central to the cycle of poverty.

There is great potential for South Africa to produce food for all but the challenges of transition remain for the onset of sustainable production and fair distribution.

So surely it’s time for all hands to the grindstone. But with economic and environmental challenges in the land of inequity where do we start? It is even difficult to get the food infrastructure right if the money and workers are there, because increasingly, environmental shifts cannot be predicted.


Further information:
We've told this story many times before, the rising cost of inflation, and the cost of food. We have covered what a basic food basket is to feed a family of 4 and how difficult it is for most South Africans to even put that kind of food on the table. But now with food prices spiraling upward, what does that mean for us? According to the Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity Group, which compiles the monthly household affordability index, the average household food basket now costs R4 609, R473 more than a year ago. I propose we take a look at my last two stories from a few years ago and the costs we looked at, and to now go and do some comparisons and to experience just how much more we are spending. To see if the rising cost of food is in line with inflation or is it exceeding.

The monthly food basket for middle income earners is more varied than that of low income earners, according to Maria Vd Merwe, Head of Association for Dietetics in SA, a household with an average income of R30 000 per month would typically spend about 20% = R6000 of their income on food, which may also include eating out. "There is a real risk of the perception that healthy eating is expensive and the lower cost and easier access and availability of junk food may lead to an increase in the consumption of processed, high fat and high sugar foods". We speak to more families on what they have to cut back on, and what can be done to stretch our ever shrinking budgets. Some are cutting out one meal a day, eating less meat, baking their own bread and rationing tinned food, and some are simply going hungry. We know that these costs will affect the poor in the most devastating way and have long term repercussions, malnutrition in children leads to poor performance at school and ultimately to a less productive adult life. The cycle of poverty and inequality then perpetuates. Rising food prices, unemployment, rising poverty is setting the climate for social and political upheaval according to Roodt.

Press Release:


The severity of the global food crisis is stretching South Africans to the limit. What can we do without - in order to continue feeding our families?

Script:


VO: I'm on a mission. One that millions of South Africans are all too familiar with... shopping for food on a rationed budget... Today, I want to see how much essential food R200 can buy. Bearing in mind, just the mere act of going to work cranks up the bills.

VO: Everyone wants to eat in a way that keeps us healthy and fit, but our shrivelling budgets are being tested - and cutting back on nutrition can lead to problems down the line.
Mervyn: It really is in the interest of every single South African that the issues around hunger is resolved. Because all our futures hang on that together.
VO: Mervyn Abrahams is programme coordinator at the Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity Group, which tracks the costs of 44 essential food items across the country, that now cost R4 609 up by R472 from last year.
Mervyn: COVID has really impacted food prices massively. We have not totally recovered. And now it is, it is the affordability crisis.
VO: But people's resilience to absorb these setbacks is wearing thin, even as the memory of lockdown begins to fade.

Masa: Tough choices - it’s either I get bread and maybe I can squeeze in six eggs.

VO: But just as we thought things couldn't get worse - we're confronted with a war that sends food prices soaring globally. The Russia-Ukraine conflict threatens a humanitarian disaster.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns - the world is facing a “severe food crisis”.
Thousands of kilometres from the battleground, South Africa is feeling the shockwave. For starters, Russia and Ukraine are major exporters of grain.
Sifiso: And that's of course resulted in wheat prices going up. It's also then resulted in massive supply chain disruptions on the back of higher oil prices.
VO: Another blow to our purses - with an expected 15 to 20% food hike looming. Economist Sifiso Skenjana is concerned that South African households are going to find it even harder to cope when 57% of people live on less than R1400 a month.
Sifiso: Households are already spending between 18 and 23% of their earnings on transport alone. And then when you add utilities, you add food and education, these people have nothing.
VO: But what of the middle-income earners - the lifeblood of the economy - who take home between R15000 and R42000 a month? A recent FNB survey reports that these workers have already spent up to 80% of their salary within the first 5 days.
Mervyn: Most of that 80% are actually going off on stop orders. So that is servicing the debt and the costs that they carry. So they left are 20%.
Sifiso: If you earn 48,750, you're in the top 1% of earners in the country. And so you've got 9% of people only who are able to afford the living standards in South Africa.
Masa: Are salaries even keeping up with these rising costs?
Sifiso: Wages aren't growing at the same pace as the price level in South Africa. And I think that's certainly going to be a challenge.
VO: Adding to the burden are electricity tariff increases of around 12% annually.
Sifiso: The kind of impact that it’s going to have around also, your disposable income, I think is going to be absolutely catastrophic.
VO: Households are feeling the squeeze. Six years ago we met estate agent Sandra Miller, who was grappling with food costs, as a single mom with 4 growing teenage boys. Her veggie patch was one of her secret weapons - today it looks slightly different.
Masa: It’s quite impressive
Sandra: Thank you
Masa: And what do we have here?
Sandra: You can see I do have my lemon. I've got mango. and then I've got my vegetables, all through summer I do not buy vegetables at all.
VO: Even though Sandra is pretty self-sustaining, things haven't become easier.
Sandra: It's like, we're in survival mode now. Twice a week, we don't eat meat, because meat, is so expensive and our portion also had to reduce. 2016, my groceries per month cost me 2000. But now I found that 4000 don't take me through the month.
Masa: Does it then cover toiletries, cleaning products?
Sandra: No, I'm talking about just food.
VO: School lunches have changed for Sandra's boys - a burger patty and cheese is now a peanut butter sandwich, and bargain shopping is a way of life // beat//
So I thought I'd finish my shopping trip by taking a leaf out of her book. With around R46 left, I made my way to the veggie shop//
VO: Outside of the food budget there are of course - toiletries.
Masa: What really stretched me - the toilet paper. Now the thing about bargain shopping is that it's actually quite expensive because to get from one shop to the other… you need petrol.
VO: And we've all been hit at the petrol pumps over the last year, with crippling increases of 41.1% for petrol and 57.5% for diesel.// But further hikes are on the horizon - Russia and Ukraine are critical to global oil and gas supplies. The knock-on effect? Most of our goods, like the basic food items I bought, are transported by road.
Mervyn: If we look globally, then the food and agricultural organizations food basket is now at the highest level it has ever been in 60 years. In South Africa, for instance, when we look at pilchards over the last year that has increased by about 13%. brown bread has increased by about 9%
Masa: If I was to have to feed let's say a family of four, all this that I've gotten here for 200 bucks really won't last me too long
Mervyn: Well, exactly, it probably will get you two or three meals. And that's the reality of most households in South Africa today.
VO: And when food is the overwhelming priority, every luxury or hobby becomes disposable.
Sandra: We used to go to Joburg theatre, take the kids to pleasure parks, but I had to cut those things out. And I was able to buy pool tables for nothing or next to nothing so now they catch their entertainment at home.
VO: These sacrifices are paying off - Sandra is now able to study for her law degree. But many people are forced to work two jobs.
Sifiso: I don't think you can sustainably at this point in time stay on the right side of that middle-class line if you don't have an additional income.
VO: Extra income is often not an option for pensioners like Hilary and Dave White, who are both in their 70s and they're counting every penny.
Hilary: Sjoh, So much.
Both my husband and I are both on pensions only. My outgoings are more than that at the moment. I'm using my savings up slowly but surely.
VO: Sharing some of Hilary's delicious homemade lemon cake, put things into perspective. You work your whole life - plan carefully for retirement, but now with costs out of control, the future is less certain.
Hilary: It's getting more and more difficult for me to think about what I buy, do and so on. So I've started thinking about making meals in bulk and freeze them into small containers.
Masa: What would you say some of the shockers have been for you?
Hilary: Oil is costing a lot more and I'm glad to say I'm not using that much because I've got the air fryer. Chicken can be cooked in 20 minutes, whereas you'll take a good hour plus in the oven. It does work out cheaper in the long run.
LINK: Cooking oil costs over 50% more than it did last year. So I should probably opt to boil this egg, right?
VO: But why has oil become so expensive?
Mervyn: We produce quite a lot of sunflower in the Free State. But we do not produce enough for local consumption. So we import from the Ukraine. The local producer would demand the same price in South Africa as what we pay to import. // And so it is imperative that we for instance try and produce as much for the local market as we possibly can.
VO: And until we do, the repercussions will not only be felt in the pantry. Many people, like Sandra and Hilary, are cutting insurance and private medical care to the bare minimum.
//Beat
But Sandra's not one to feel beaten down - she introduces me to another inflation-busting secret weapon - thrifting…
Sandra: laughs
Masa: R45?!
VO: And more pros of being self-sustainable.
Masa: Is this just from today?
Sandra: Ja, this is today, and it’s just from these two chickens. For a while now I haven’t bought eggs.
VO: The stark truth is most South Africans are struggling to be self-sufficient and the level of acute malnutrition in the country is alarming. According to STATS SA, 25% of girl children and about 30% of boy children under the age of five are stunted.
Mervyn: Now, this is a cognitive impairment, which is a direct result of chronic undernutrition.It definitely has an impact on our educational outcomes. It has an impact on the disease burden. It has an impact on our economic growth.
VO: Deepening the poverty trap, are external forces and a war that may go on for months or even years. The aftermath will be felt for generations to come.

VO: School lunches have changed for Sandra's boys - a burger patty and cheese is now a peanut butter sandwich, and bargain shopping is a way of life // beat// So I thought I'd finish my shopping trip by taking a leaf out of her book. With around R46 left, I made my way to the veggie shop// VO: Outside of the food budget there are of course - toiletries. Masa: What really stretched me - the toilet paper. Now the thing about bargain shopping is that it's actually quite expensive because to get from one shop to the other… you need petrol. VO: And we've all been hit at the petrol pumps over the last year, with crippling increases of 41.1% for petrol and 57.5% for diesel.// But further hikes are on the horizon - Russia and Ukraine are critical to global oil and gas supplies. The knock-on effect? Most of our goods, like the basic food items I bought, are transported by road. Mervyn: If we look globally, then the food and agricultural organizations food basket is now at the highest level it has ever been in 60 years. In South Africa, for instance, when we look at pilchards over the last year that has increased by about 13%. brown bread has increased by about 9% Masa: If I was to have to feed let's say a family of four, all this that I've gotten here for 200 bucks really won't last me too long Mervyn: Well, exactly, it probably will get you two or three meals. And that's the reality of most households in South Africa today. VO: And when food is the overwhelming priority, every luxury or hobby becomes disposable. Sandra: We used to go to Joburg theatre, take the kids to pleasure parks, but I had to cut those things out. And I was able to buy pool tables for nothing or next to nothing so now they catch their entertainment at home. VO: These sacrifices are paying off - Sandra is now able to study for her law degree. But many people are forced to work two jobs. Sifiso: I don't think you can sustainably at this point in time stay on the right side of that middle-class line if you don't have an additional income. VO: Extra income is often not an option for pensioners like Hilary and Dave White, who are both in their 70s and they're counting every penny. Hilary: Sjoh, So much. Both my husband and I are both on pensions only. My outgoings are more than that at the moment. I'm using my savings up slowly but surely. VO: Sharing some of Hilary's delicious homemade lemon cake, put things into perspective. You work your whole life - plan carefully for retirement, but now with costs out of control, the future is less certain. Hilary: It's getting more and more difficult for me to think about what I buy, do and so on. So I've started thinking about making meals in bulk and freeze them into small containers. Masa: What would you say some of the shockers have been for you? Hilary: Oil is costing a lot more and I'm glad to say I'm not using that much because I've got the air fryer. Chicken can be cooked in 20 minutes, whereas you'll take a good hour plus in the oven. It does work out cheaper in the long run. LINK: Cooking oil costs over 50% more than it did last year. So I should probably opt to boil this egg, right? VO: But why has oil become so expensive? Mervyn: We produce quite a lot of sunflower in the Free State. But we do not produce enough for local consumption. So we import from the Ukraine. The local producer would demand the same price in South Africa as what we pay to import. // And so it is imperative that we for instance try and produce as much for the local market as we possibly can. VO: And until we do, the repercussions will not only be felt in the pantry. Many people, like Sandra and Hilary, are cutting insurance and private medical care to the bare minimum. //Beat But Sandra's not one to feel beaten down - she introduces me to another inflation-busting secret weapon - thrifting… Sandra: laughs Masa: R45?! VO: And more pros of being self-sustainable. Masa: Is this just from today? Sandra: Ja, this is today, and it’s just from these two chickens. For a while now I haven’t bought eggs. VO: The stark truth is most South Africans are struggling to be self-sufficient and the level of acute malnutrition in the country is alarming. According to STATS SA, 25% of girl children and about 30% of boy children under the age of five are stunted. Mervyn: Now, this is a cognitive impairment, which is a direct result of chronic undernutrition.It definitely has an impact on our educational outcomes. It has an impact on the disease burden. It has an impact on our economic growth. VO: Deepening the poverty trap, are external forces and a war that may go on for months or even years. The aftermath will be felt for generations to come.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Spiraling food prices can only deepen the poverty trap, lower nutrition, inhibit education - prospects are dwindling for the poor. What steps can South Africans take to reverse the hunger trend?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Nutrition is at the heart of a healthy life cycle. Get it right and society can thrive. But get it wrong and the cycle of poverty gets harder to break. The prospects this year are looking bleak for the South African food chain. "Economists are predicting that food prices will rise between 15 and 20% in the coming months. Pushing low income earners to the brink and stretching middle class pockets further". Compared with a year ago consumers are paying nearly 12% more for basic food items, 41.1% more for petrol and 57.5% more for diesel. (According to economist Dawie Roodt). Much of the escalation of prices in our shops is linked to the break down in supplies of commodities like grain and fuel related to the war in Ukraine. So how does one combat these devastating effects on our most basic needs? Must we change our diets? Export less food or raise the taxes on food exports to become more self-sufficient?
metadata.Summary: Society’s ills are reflected by what we eat. We take a look at how malnutrition is central to the cycle of poverty. There is great potential for South Africa to produce food for all but the challenges of transition remain for the onset of sustainable production and fair distribution. So surely it’s time for all hands to the grindstone. But with economic and environmental challenges in the land of inequity where do we start? It is even difficult to get the food infrastructure right if the money and workers are there, because increasingly, environmental shifts cannot be predicted.
metadata.Further information: We've told this story many times before, the rising cost of inflation, and the cost of food. We have covered what a basic food basket is to feed a family of 4 and how difficult it is for most South Africans to even put that kind of food on the table. But now with food prices spiraling upward, what does that mean for us? According to the Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity Group, which compiles the monthly household affordability index, the average household food basket now costs R4 609, R473 more than a year ago. I propose we take a look at my last two stories from a few years ago and the costs we looked at, and to now go and do some comparisons and to experience just how much more we are spending. To see if the rising cost of food is in line with inflation or is it exceeding. The monthly food basket for middle income earners is more varied than that of low income earners, according to Maria Vd Merwe, Head of Association for Dietetics in SA, a household with an average income of R30 000 per month would typically spend about 20% = R6000 of their income on food, which may also include eating out. "There is a real risk of the perception that healthy eating is expensive and the lower cost and easier access and availability of junk food may lead to an increase in the consumption of processed, high fat and high sugar foods". We speak to more families on what they have to cut back on, and what can be done to stretch our ever shrinking budgets. Some are cutting out one meal a day, eating less meat, baking their own bread and rationing tinned food, and some are simply going hungry. We know that these costs will affect the poor in the most devastating way and have long term repercussions, malnutrition in children leads to poor performance at school and ultimately to a less productive adult life. The cycle of poverty and inequality then perpetuates. Rising food prices, unemployment, rising poverty is setting the climate for social and political upheaval according to Roodt. Case Studies: Middle income family and family whose children are malnourished – what are they cutting back on? Are feeding schemes making a difference? Experts: Dr at Sebokeng who is seeing more and more cases of malnutrition Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity Group – including the question are feeding schemes going to keep up with increased food costs?
